name: When Students May Use AI in Math
title: When Students May Use AI in Math
answer: When students may use AI in math is a decision a teacher makes for each task, in the same way math teachers have long set their own rules for calculators. Tasks carry clear AI use levels, so a fluency quiz can be marked no AI while a data project can allow AI for organizing and graphing. The purpose is to remove guessing about what is permitted, because unclear rules are where integrity trouble tends to start.

sections.body: Math teachers have always decided when a calculator is allowed, and the book argues that AI needs the same kind of rule rather than one blanket answer for a whole school. Some assignments exist to build basic skills that students must do by hand, while others aim at problem solving where a tool can carry the routine steps. The AI use levels described in Chapter 3 are applied task by task, so the level matches the purpose of the work. The problem this solves is confusion, since students and families otherwise have to guess whether a tool is permitted on a given night. Clear levels tell everyone what the task is actually for.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom the teacher labels each assignment with its AI use level before it goes home. A fluency quiz might be marked no AI, so the student works alone, while a data project might allow AI for organizing and graphing. A student who sees that a project permits AI for checking work knows how to use the tool honestly, and a parent who sees a no AI mark knows the child should not have help. The text presents this as an approach for Kindergarten through 12th grade and does not split the levels by grade band. What changes across the grades is the task, not the rule.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its support is the long-standing parallel with calculators, which teachers already decide on, and the reasoning that clear rules cut down on guessing. The claim that unclear rules are where integrity trouble usually begins is presented as the book's own observation, not as a finding from a study. Readers should treat the levels as a practical convention a school adopts, not as a demonstrated result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The decisions stay with the teacher. Math teachers set the level for each task, just as they have set calculator rules, and the text does not hand that judgment to a tool or a policy document. The risk it names is integrity, because a bare answer gives no clue about its source, so a submitted answer tells the teacher little on its own. That is why the written steps matter more than they once did, with the teacher able to follow the reasoning and find where it went wrong. Many math teachers now give most of the credit for the process, which also makes it easier to see whether a student understands the method.
